To reimburse someone means to pay them back money they already spent — usually because they spent it on your behalf, or because of something you caused.

The most important thing to understand is the sequence of events:

  1. Someone spends their own money first.
  2. Then you pay them back that same amount.

Without that sequence — money spent first, money returned later — the word doesn't apply.
A Simple Example to Lock It In

Imagine your colleague buys printer ink for the office using his own wallet. It costs $30. Since he bought it for work, the company pays him back that $30.

"The company reimbursed him for the printer ink."

He is out of pocket → the company pays him back → he is reimbursed. That's it.

The structure of the verb is almost always:

[Person/Organisation] reimburses [Person] for [Expense]

Here are the most natural real-world situations:

1. Employer → Employee
This is the most common context. Employees often spend their own money on work-related things — travel, meals, supplies — and then submit receipts so the company can pay them back.

"My employer reimbursed me for the flight tickets."
"She was reimbursed for her hotel stay during the business trip."

2. Insurance Company → Policyholder
You pay a medical or repair bill out of your own pocket first, then the insurance company pays you back.

"The insurance company reimbursed him for the hospital bill."

3. Government → Citizen
Governments sometimes refund people for certain approved expenses, like healthcare or education costs.

"The government reimbursed families for tutoring expenses."

4. One Person → Another Person
In everyday life, if a friend pays for something on your behalf, you reimburse them later.

"She paid for my train ticket, and I reimbursed her the next day."

You can only use "reimburse" when real money was actually spent first. The reimbursement is specifically the return of that spent amount.

If no money was spent yet, you wouldn't use this word. For example, you wouldn't say "I will reimburse you before you buy it." That makes no sense with this word — the spending must come first.

The verb "reimburse" is used in a few very consistent patterns. Learn these and you'll use the word correctly every time.

  • Reimburse someone for something:

"The company reimbursed her for the taxi fare."

  • Reimburse someone's expenses:

"We will reimburse your travel expenses."

  • Be reimbursed (passive voice — very common):

"All volunteers will be reimbursed for their costs."
"He was never reimbursed for the damage."

  • Reimburse someone in full:

"She was reimbursed in full after submitting the receipts."
("In full" means the entire amount was paid back, not just part of it.)
How It Differs From Similar Words

Reimburse vs. Refund
A refund is when a store or seller gives your money back — usually because you returned a product or a service was cancelled. The relationship is between a buyer and a seller.
"The shop refunded me because the jacket was torn."

A reimbursement is between two people/parties where one paid on behalf of the other — not a buyer-seller return situation.
"My employer reimbursed me for buying the jacket I needed for the work event."

Reimburse vs. Compensate
Compensate is broader. It covers paying someone for loss, damage, suffering, or inconvenience — not just for money they spent. You can compensate someone for their time, their pain, or their lost opportunity.
"The airline compensated passengers for the 10-hour delay." (This could be vouchers, upgrades, or money — not necessarily a specific amount they spent.)

Reimburse is more precise — it's specifically about paying back an exact amount someone spent.

Reimburse vs. Pay back / Repay
Pay back and repay usually refer to returning borrowed money (a loan, a debt). The money was lent, not spent on someone's behalf.
"I borrowed $50 from her and paid her back on Friday."

Reimburse implies the money was spent for a purpose (usually for you or your organisation), not just borrowed.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Reimburse" is a formal word. You'll see it a lot in professional, business, legal, and financial contexts — expense forms, insurance policies, employment contracts, and official letters.

In casual everyday conversation, people tend to say "pay you back" instead:

  • Formal: "You will be reimbursed within 10 business days."
  • Casual: "I'll pay you back tomorrow."

Both mean the same thing, but "reimburse" carries a professional, official tone.

If you ever want to check whether "reimburse" is the right word, ask yourself two questions:

  1. Did someone already spend their own money? ✅
  2. Are they being paid back that amount? ✅

If both answers are yes — that's reimbursement.
